item.title: How do you set up a martha tent for mushrooms?
item.description: Size the fan for 4 to 6 air changes an hour, put the humidifier low and the sensor mid height, run light 12 h on a timer, and group species by target.
item.content:encoded:
A martha tent is a wire shelf in a clear zip up cover with three add ons: an ultrasonic humidifier on the bottom shelf, a fan on a timer, and a light on a timer. Aim the mist into open space, never at a block, and put the humidity sensor at mid height out of the mist. Size the fan for 4 to 6 fresh air changes an hour while oysters fruit, the University of California number. For a 70 x 50 x 160 cm tent (560 L) that averages 37 to 56 L of air a minute, about 1.3 to 2 CFM, so a fan that really moves 20 CFM only needs 40 seconds every 10 minutes, which is the fan cycle in our pearl oyster profile. Run light 12 hours a day at 50 to 300 lux. Then fill the tent with species that want the same numbers: our oyster profiles fruit at 86 to 88% humidity, lion's mane at 90% and 17 °C, chestnut and nameko at 92 to 93%, and pink and golden oyster fruit at 21 to 24 °C while the rest fruit at 14 to 17 °C.

What is a martha tent, and when is it worth building?

A martha tent is a small greenhouse shelf, usually four or five wire shelves inside a clear plastic cover with a zip front, turned into a fruiting chamber. The name stuck from the first builds on a store bought portable closet, and now it means any shelf in a clear cover. On its own it is just a humid box. It becomes a fruiting chamber when you add a humidifier, a fan and a light, and put the humidifier and fan on controllers so they run without you.

It fits between a single grow kit and a countertop smart chamber. Our grow kit vs monotub vs smart chamber guide puts the shelf tent in the "biggest harvest for the money" group, with uneven conditions between shelves as the main thing that goes wrong. Build one when one block at a time feels too small and you have floor space near an outlet, ideally near a window or vent you can exhaust to.

The hard part is not the shelf. It is getting humidity, fresh air and light right at the same time, in a box that is far bigger than a kit and far leakier than a sealed chamber. The rest of this post gives you numbers for each one.

What size martha tent do you need, and how do you work out its volume?

Measure the inside of your cover, not the box it came in. Volume decides how big the humidifier has to be and how much fan you need.

Volume in liters is length x width x height in centimeters, divided by 1,000. For a worked example, take a tent measuring 70 x 50 x 160 cm inside:

  • 70 x 50 x 160 = 560,000 cubic centimeters, which is 560 L, or about 19.8 cubic feet.
  • That is more than fifteen times the 36 L chamber in the worked example on our fresh air calculator.

Plan the shelf load with air in mind. Leave a hand's width between blocks and between blocks and the cover so the fan's air and the mist can reach every side. Oysters fruit out of the holes in the bag, so face the holes toward open space, not toward the cover or the next bag.

Where should the humidifier go in a martha tent?

Put an ultrasonic humidifier on the bottom of the tent and aim the mist up into the open middle of the tent, not at a block. A SARE funded oyster guide says the hard part of humidifying is getting the air wet without spraying the mushrooms, because mushrooms soak up any water that lands on them and go soggy (SARE and FungiAlly). Mist that lands as drops is a problem; mist that hangs in the air is the goal.

Rules that keep it working:

  • Leave the bottom shelf empty, or use it only for blocks well out of the mist path. The block nearest the outlet will get wet first.
  • Keep the humidifier out of standing water. Set the tent on a tray to catch condensation, and set the humidifier up on something so it does not sit in the puddle it makes.
  • Use distilled water. The EPA says ultrasonic humidifiers are very efficient at putting tap water minerals into the air as white dust, and that mineral scale in the tank can be a breeding ground for microorganisms. Distilled water has the least mineral content (EPA). In a closed tent, that dust lands on your mushrooms.
  • Clean it on a schedule. The EPA says to empty and refill a portable humidifier daily and scrub it every third day. The CPSC warns that bacteria and fungi grow in dirty humidifier tanks and come out in the mist (CPSC). A tent is a warm, wet place, so a dirty tank seeds the same air your blocks are breathing.
  • Plug it into a GFCI outlet. Water, mist and power cords share a small space. The CPSC says a GFCI shuts off power when as little as 0.006 amps leaks to ground, and recommends GFCI protection where electrical equipment is near water (CPSC). If the outlet is not a GFCI, a plug in GFCI adapter does the job.

How do you size a humidifier for a martha tent?

There is no reliable liters per hour rule, because how fast a tent loses moisture depends on how leaky the cover is, how dry the room is and how much fan you run. Test it instead, with the tent empty:

  1. Set the fan cycle you plan to use (next section).
  2. Turn the humidifier on through its controller with the target you plan to fruit at.
  3. Watch the reading through a few fan cycles.

A humidifier that is big enough pulls the tent back to target well before the next fan run starts. One that never reaches the target, or only gets there with the fan off, is too small or the cover leaks too much. One that overshoots far past the target before it shuts off is too strong for the space, or is too close to the sensor.

What humidity should a martha tent run at?

Set it to the species, not to a general number. A University of California grower guide gives 95% for oyster pinhead initiation and 85 to 92% while they crop (UC ANR). The SARE guide gives 80 to 90%, close to 90% to start pins (SARE and FungiAlly). Our profiles sit inside those ranges and step down from pinning to fruiting, the way our humidity and fresh air guide explains.

The bigger mistake in tents is the control band, not the target. A wide band, such as on at 80% and off at 90%, makes the tent swing ten points every cycle. Our own firmware turns the humidifier on 1.5 points under target and off 0.5 points over, with at least 90 seconds on and 60 seconds off so it does not chatter (OpenShrooly controls.yaml). Copy that idea on whatever controller you use: the narrowest band it allows, with a minimum on and off time if it has one.

Where should the humidity sensor go?

At mid height, near the blocks, out of the mist stream. A sensor in the plume reads near 100% and shuts the humidifier off while the top shelf dries out. A sensor on the top shelf against a warm ceiling reads lower than the blocks feel.

Check the sensor before you trust it. Seal it in a jar with a damp paste of table salt and water for 8 to 12 hours at steady room temperature. Saturated salt holds the air at about 75% at 25 °C (Greenspan, NIST). If your sensor reads 70% or 80% in that jar, it is 5 points off, and so is your tent. The humidity and fresh air guide has the full method.

If you can, put a second sensor on the top shelf for the first grow. The top and bottom of a tent rarely match, and the gap tells you whether to move blocks or move the sensor.

How much fresh air does a martha tent need?

Size the fan with air changes per hour. One air change moves as much air as the tent holds. The University of California guide lists 4 fresh air changes an hour while oyster pins form and 4 to 6 an hour while they crop, with carbon dioxide under 600 ppm, and none during spawn run (UC ANR). The SARE guide says to keep carbon dioxide under 800 ppm, to change all the air in a fruiting room at least every 10 minutes, which is 6 changes an hour, and that above 1,200 ppm fruiting can be inhibited (SARE and FungiAlly).

For the 560 L example tent:

TargetAir per hourAverage flowAverage flow in CFM
4 air changes an hour2,240 L37 L per minute1.3 CFM
6 air changes an hour3,360 L56 L per minute2.0 CFM

That average is tiny. A small fan running nonstop would blow the humidity out of the tent, which is why you run it in short bursts on a timer. The math is the same one the fresh air calculator uses: air changes per hour equals fan flow per hour times the share of each cycle the fan is on, divided by the tent volume. Enter your tent size and your fan's flow there, pick the species, and it fills in the profile's fan cycle and shows the air changes you get.

What fan cycle should you use for each species?

Here is what each profile's fruiting fan cycle gives in the 560 L tent if your fan really moves 20 CFM (566 L per minute) at full speed. Use full speed in a tent. The fan speed percent in a profile is for a small chamber fan.

MushroomFruiting fan cycle in the profileFan onAir changes an hour in a 560 L tent at 20 CFM
Pearl oyster, blue oyster, golden oyster, pink oyster40 s every 10 min6.7%4.0
Shiitake35 s every 12 min4.9%2.9
Chestnut, pioppino30 s every 15 min3.3%2.0
Lion's mane, nameko, beech25 s every 18 min2.3%1.4
King oyster25 s every 25 min1.7%1.0

So the oyster profile cycle lands right on the low end of the University of California number, and the slower species get less air, which is what their profiles ask for. If your fan moves more or less than 20 CFM, scale the run time by the same ratio. A 40 CFM fan needs half the seconds.

Two cautions. A fan rarely moves its rated flow once it pushes through a filter or a small hole, so measured flow is usually lower than the label. And a full tent holds a lot of substrate in little air. The University of California and SARE numbers are for grow rooms full of blocks, and a packed martha tent is closer to that than a one block chamber is. Start at the profile cycle and let the mushrooms correct you: long stems and small caps mean more air, as our leggy stems guide covers, and dry or cracked caps mean more humidity.

Where should the fan go?

Mount the fan through the cover low on one side and leave a filtered exhaust opening high on the opposite side, so each burst sweeps across the shelves. Do not point it straight at a block. Short, frequent bursts beat long, rare ones: every burst pulls humidity down, because room air is drier than fruiting air, and short bursts give the humidifier time to recover, as the fresh air calculator explains.

Why exhaust a martha tent outside the room?

Spores. The SARE guide says oyster mushrooms are known for their heavy spore load and calls for routine cleaning and a mask in the fruiting room (SARE and FungiAlly). Oyster spores have caused allergic lung inflammation in mushroom workers, and one clinical report found that growing oysters as a hobby was enough to cause the sensitivity (European Respiratory Journal 1993; Occupational Medicine 1998). A tent full of fruiting oysters in a bedroom puts those spores into the room you sleep in. Duct the exhaust out a window or into a space nobody sleeps in, wear a mask when you open the tent to harvest, and harvest oysters while the cap edges still roll under, which the SARE guide says also limits how many spores they release.

How much light does a martha tent need, and for how long?

Not much, but on a schedule. Penn State's oyster production guide gives 50 to 300 lux of cool white light after spawn run (Royse, Penn State). Most of our profiles run 12 hours a day at about 92 lux, starting at 8:00. Lion's mane runs 190 lux. Bright light is not better: our do mushrooms need light post covers why indirect light is fine and direct sun is not, since it heats and dries the block, and which species want something different.

Martha specific details:

  • Wire shelves shade each other. A light on top lights the top shelf and leaves the bottom in shadow. Run a strip down the inside front or both sides of the tent so every shelf sees some light.
  • Use a plug in timer. Set 12 hours on, 12 off, so the schedule does not depend on you or the room lights.
  • Keep it cool. A low output LED strip is plenty. A hot lamp warms the top of the tent and dries it.
  • Keep colonizing blocks out. Our profiles keep colonization dark, and the University of California guide lists total darkness for oyster spawn run (UC ANR). Finish colonizing in a dark spot, then move blocks into the tent.

Which mushrooms can share one martha tent?

One tent has one humidity target, one fan timer and one room temperature, so fill it with species that want the same numbers. A martha tent has no heating or cooling, so the room sets the temperature. These are the fruiting numbers from our profiles:

MushroomPinningFruiting humidityFruiting temperatureLight
Blue oyster94%, 15 °C87%14 °C (57 °F)12 h, 92 lux
Pearl oyster93%, 18 °C88%16 °C (61 °F)12 h, 92 lux
King oyster90%, 16 °C82%15 °C (59 °F)12 h, 92 lux
Lion's mane94%, 18 °C90%17 °C (63 °F)12 h, 190 lux
Beech94%, 16 °C90%15 °C (59 °F)12 h, 92 lux
Pioppino92%, 17 °C86%16 °C (61 °F)12 h, 92 lux
ShiitakeFruits in one stage85%16 °C (61 °F)12 h, 92 lux
Chestnut95%, 16 °C92%15 °C (59 °F)12 h, 92 lux
Nameko95%, 15 °C93%14 °C (57 °F)12 h, 92 lux
Golden oyster93%, 22 °C87%21 °C (70 °F)12 h, 92 lux
Pink oyster92%, 24 °C86%24 °C (75 °F)12 h, 92 lux

Groupings that work from that table:

  • Cool room oysters: pearl and blue oyster together, at about 87 to 88% and 14 to 16 °C, on the 40 seconds every 10 minutes fan cycle. Pioppino and shiitake sit close on humidity and temperature and get by on the same tent with a little more air than they need.
  • Damp and gentle: lion's mane and beech at 90% and 15 to 17 °C, on 25 seconds every 18 minutes. Chestnut and nameko want 92 to 93%, so add them only if your tent holds the higher number.
  • Warm room: golden and pink oyster at 86 to 87% and 21 to 24 °C. Put this tent in a warm room. In a 15 °C garage in November, pink oyster is the wrong pick.
  • On its own: king oyster fruits at 82%, the driest of the group, and wants the least air. In a shared tent it sits in wetter air than its profile asks for, so give it its own tent or a spot farthest from the humidifier.

If you mix, set the tent to the species with the least room for error. Our lion's mane profile says to cut fresh air and raise humidity if the spines yellow or brown, and oysters go leggy without air. A mixed tent of lion's mane and pearl oyster means running the oyster fan cycle and keeping humidity at the lion's mane number, then watching both.

How to set up a martha tent, step by step

  1. Assemble the shelf and cover on a tray in a room near the fruiting temperature of the species you plan to grow, close to a GFCI outlet and a window or vent for exhaust.
  2. Measure the inside and work out the volume in liters: length x width x height in cm, divided by 1,000.
  3. Cut a fan hole low on one side and a filtered exhaust hole high on the other side.
  4. Put the ultrasonic humidifier on the bottom, raised out of standing water, with the mist aimed into the open middle of the tent. Fill it with distilled water.
  5. Put the humidity sensor at mid height, near where the blocks will sit, out of the mist stream. Check it in a salt jar first.
  6. Plug the humidifier into a humidity controller set to the profile's target with the narrowest band it allows.
  7. Enter your tent size and fan flow in the fresh air calculator, pick the species, and set the fan timer to the cycle it shows.
  8. Mount a low output LED strip down the front or sides and put it on a timer for 12 hours a day.
  9. Run the tent empty for a day and watch humidity through several fan cycles. Fix the humidifier size or the band before any blocks go in.
  10. Move fully colonized blocks in with space between them and holes facing open air. Change humidity and fan from the pinning to the fruiting numbers on the day the profile says.

What goes wrong with a martha tent?

  • Water pooling on caps, yellow or slimy spots: too much mist landing on the mushrooms or too little air moving. Aim the humidifier away and add air before you lower humidity, the order our humidity and fresh air guide recommends.
  • Dry, cracked caps on the top shelf: the top of the tent is drier than the sensor. Move the sensor up or the blocks down, or add a second sensor.
  • Long stems, small caps, coral shaped oysters: too little fresh air. Lengthen the fan run.
  • Humidity crashes after every fan run and never recovers: humidifier too small, cover too leaky, or fan bursts too long. Shorter, more frequent bursts move the same air with smaller drops.
  • White dust on everything: tap water in an ultrasonic humidifier. Switch to distilled.
  • Musty smell or slime in the humidifier tank: clean it every third day and change the water daily.

If you would rather not tune a humidifier and timer by hand, a small automated chamber does the same job for one or two blocks. Our ESP32 fruiting chamber build uses the same control logic and runs a profile by stage.

FAQ

How many air changes does a martha tent need?

For oysters, 4 to 6 fresh air changes an hour while fruiting, the University of California number. In a 560 L tent that is 37 to 56 L of air a minute on average. A fan that really moves 20 CFM running 40 seconds every 10 minutes gives about 4.

Where do you put the humidifier in a martha tent?

On the bottom, raised out of standing water, with the mist aimed into the open middle of the tent and not at any block. Put the humidity sensor at mid height, out of the mist stream.

What humidity should a martha tent be?

It depends on the species. Our oyster profiles fruit at 86 to 88%, lion's mane and beech at 90%, chestnut and nameko at 92 to 93%, and king oyster at 82%. Pinning runs a few points higher.

Can you use tap water in a martha tent humidifier?

You can, but the EPA says ultrasonic humidifiers spread tap water minerals as white dust and that mineral scale can grow microorganisms. Distilled water avoids both.

Does a martha tent need a light?

It needs some light on a regular schedule. Penn State gives 50 to 300 lux for oysters, and our profiles run 12 hours a day at about 92 lux for most species. A low output LED strip on a timer is enough.

Is a martha tent a greenhouse fruiting chamber?

Yes. It is a small indoor greenhouse shelf with a humidifier, fan and light added. The same setup steps apply to any shelf in a clear cover.

Sources

  • UC Agriculture and Natural Resources, Cultivating Mushrooms on Small Family Farms, for 4 fresh air changes an hour while oyster pins form, 4 to 6 while they crop, carbon dioxide under 600 ppm, no fresh air and total darkness during spawn run, 95% for pinhead initiation and 85 to 92% while cropping
  • SARE and FungiAlly, Growing Oyster Mushrooms, for humidifying without spraying mushrooms, 80 to 90% humidity and close to 90% for pins, carbon dioxide under 800 ppm, all the air changed at least every 10 minutes, inhibited fruiting above 1,200 ppm, the heavy oyster spore load with a mask in the fruiting room, and a rolled cap edge limiting spore release
  • Royse, Cultivation of Oyster Mushrooms, Penn State College of Agricultural Sciences, for 50 to 300 lux of cool white light after spawn run
  • US EPA, Use and Care of Home Humidifiers, for ultrasonic humidifiers spreading tap water minerals, scale as a breeding ground for microorganisms, distilled water, daily refills and cleaning every third day
  • US CPSC, Dirty Humidifiers May Cause Health Problems, Publication 5046, for bacteria and fungi in humidifier tanks released in the mist
  • US CPSC, GFCI Fact Sheet, for GFCI protection near water and the 0.006 amp trip level
  • Greenspan 1977, Humidity Fixed Points of Binary Saturated Aqueous Solutions, Journal of Research of the NBS 81A (NIST), for saturated salt at about 75% at 25 °C
  • Extrinsic allergic alveolitis caused by spores of the oyster mushroom Pleurotus ostreatus, European Respiratory Journal 1993, for allergic lung inflammation from oyster spores and hobby growing being enough to sensitize
  • Mushroom worker's lung resulting from indoor cultivation of Pleurotus ostreatus, Occupational Medicine 48 (1998), for an outbreak in indoor oyster growers
  • OpenShrooly firmware, controls.yaml, for the humidifier turning on 1.5 points under target and off 0.5 over, with 90 seconds minimum on and 60 seconds minimum off
  • Our fresh air calculator, for the air change formula, the 36 L example chamber and short fan bursts letting humidity recover
  • Our humidity and fresh air guide, for the 8 to 12 hour salt jar check and adding air before lowering humidity
  • Our grow profiles for pearl oyster, blue oyster, golden oyster, pink oyster, king oyster, lion's mane, beech, pioppino, shiitake, chestnut and nameko, for every pinning and fruiting humidity, temperature, light and fan cycle in the tables, the 8:00 light start, dark colonization and the lion's mane note on yellow or brown spines
  • The 560 L, 2,240 L, 3,360 L, 37 and 56 L per minute, 1.3 and 2.0 CFM, fan on percentages and air changes in this post are our arithmetic from the formula above, with 1 CFM = 28.3 L per minute

item.title: Why is my lion's mane turning pink, yellow or brown?
item.description: Pink lion's mane is light stress, yellow is age or dry air, brown is bruising or warm storage. What each means and how to fix the next flush.
item.content:encoded:
Pink on a young lion's mane is a stress color that depends on strain and light. A 2025 study saw it under 500 lux for 24 hours a day at 17 to 18 °C, and got white heads at 200 lux or less on a 12 hour cycle. Yellow means the head is aging or the air is too dry or drafty, so pick it now, because yellowing heads can taste bitter. Brown is browning from age, bruised spines or warm storage. At 21 °C (70 °F) harvested lion's mane changed color past the "considerable" line by day 4, while at 5 °C (41 °F) it stayed close to white for a week. A firm, fresh smelling head with a pink blush or a few yellow tips is a quality issue you can cook or trim. A slimy, sour smelling or moldy one goes in the compost.

What each lion's mane color means

Lion's mane should be white. Every other color is the mushroom telling you something about light, age, air or handling. The trick is that the same color can show up for two different reasons, so look at where it is and when it showed up.

ColorWhere and whenMost likely causeWhat to do
Pink or peach blushYoung head, fades a little as it maturesLight stress, strain, cool roomCut light to about 200 lux, 12 h a day
Pale yellow, spine tipsMature head, long spinesAgeHarvest now
Yellow on the side facing a fan or ventAny age, one sideDry or drafty airLess fresh air, more humidity
Yellow, wet or slimy patchesAny age, with drips on the bagToo wet, too little airflowMist less, move more air
Brown spots or streaksWhere it was touched or pressedBruisingTrim and cook soon
Brown all over, after pickingIn the fridge or on the counterStorage browningStore colder and use sooner
Brown, dry, crusty tipsOn the blockVery dry airRaise humidity

The rest of this post walks through each one with the numbers behind it.

Why is my lion's mane turning pink?

Pink on lion's mane is mostly a light and strain reaction, not rot. The best data on it comes from a 2025 study at the Czech University of Life Sciences that grew four lion's mane strains (Jozifek et al. 2025):

  • One of the four strains stayed pure white in every trial. The other three showed pink while the heads were young.
  • The pink got slightly weaker as the heads matured.
  • Their grow room ran 17 to 18 °C with 500 lux of light 24 hours a day. Even the control bags, with nothing added to the substrate, came out slightly pink.
  • When they dropped the light to 200 lux or less on a 12 hour cycle, the heads came out white. A run at only 35 lux, even with light on all 24 hours, was also completely white.
  • The authors name the cool temperature, high light and nonstop light as possible causes and call the pink a possible stress reaction that depends on the strain. They note other researchers grew lion's mane under 1,000 lux without any pink, which points back at strain.

The pink in that study got stronger when they added selenium to the substrate, and an older study also saw lion's mane go white pink when selenium salts were added (Niedzielski et al. 2014). A store kit or a normal hardwood block has no added selenium, so at home the lever you control is light.

Our lion's mane profile is built around that result. It runs 12 hours of light a day at about 200 lux (190 lux in the profile) and keeps colonization fully dark. Our dense white heads profile goes further, at about 46 lux, for growers who want shade and tight heads. Its notes say a cooler room can still give a faint pink blush.

Is pink lion's mane safe to eat?

The study treats pink as a color response to growing conditions, not as spoilage. If the head is firm, dry to the touch and smells mild and fresh, the pink is a looks issue. Judge it the way you would any fresh mushroom: by firmness, smell and slime, covered in the section on when to throw it out below. Pink is not the same as the slow browning and softening of an old head.

Why is my lion's mane turning yellow?

Yellow has three different causes, and where it shows up tells you which one.

Yellow spine tips on a big head means age. Lion's mane starts white and turns yellowish, then brown, as it ages (Silva et al. 2025). The Minnesota DNR says lion's mane is best eaten white and that yellowing means aging and can taste bitter (Minnesota DNR). Our profile note is to harvest when the spines lengthen but before they yellow. If yours is yellowing now, cut it today. Next flush, pick a day or two sooner.

Yellow on one side means dry or moving air. Our profile's chamber note is direct about this: too much fresh air yellows the spines, and if the spines brown or yellow, cut fresh air and raise humidity a little. The profile runs the fan only 25 seconds every 18 minutes while fruiting, at 90% humidity. A kit right next to a heater vent, a window draft or a desk fan gets far more moving air than that.

Yellow, wet patches mean too much water. NCAT's ATTRA guide, a USDA funded grower program, says yellow patches or slimy spots with constant condensation mean humidity is too high or airflow too low, and links them to bacterial blotch (NCAT ATTRA 2026). That yellow looks glossy and wet, not dry and papery. Mist the air, not the head, and give it a little more air movement.

Why is my lion's mane turning brown?

Brown is browning: enzymes in the mushroom react with its own phenolic compounds once tissue is damaged or aging. In lion's mane, a 2025 storage study found the activity of the browning enzymes polyphenol oxidase, tyrosinase and laccase rose sharply during storage (Postharvest Biology and Technology 2025). Three things set it off.

Bruising. Lion's mane spines are very tender. A study on fresh lion's mane browning notes they are easily damaged during harvest and storage, which leads to browning (IIR 2016). Brown spots where you held it, pressed it against the bag or stacked it are bruises. Handle the head by the base, not the spines.

Warm storage. This is the big one after picking. A 2025 study stored harvested lion's mane at 5, 13 and 21 °C for up to 14 days (Silva et al. 2025):

Stored atWeight lossColor change by day 4Condition
5 °C (41 °F)About 8% by day 73.0, stayed under 7 all weekMicrobe counts acceptable until day 7
13 °C (55 °F)Past 10% by day 46.1Middle ground
21 °C (70 °F)About 28% in 2 days13.5Visible spoilage by day 7

The color change number is a standard lab measure where 3 to 6 is noticeable, 6 to 12 is significant and over 12 is considerable. The authors also found lion's mane browned faster than gray oyster mushrooms even under refrigeration, so it is a mushroom to eat early. NCAT gives the same advice from the farm side: cool mushrooms fast to 34 to 38 °F (1 to 3 °C), store them in a paper bag or vented container, and do not seal them in plastic (NCAT ATTRA 2026).

Dry air on the block. Brown, crusty tips on a head that is still growing usually mean the air dried them out. That is the same moisture problem as dry, cracked caps on other species, and NCAT says lion's mane is especially sensitive to low humidity (NCAT ATTRA 2026).

When is discolored lion's mane still good to cook?

Color alone does not decide it. Firmness, smell and slime do.

  • Keep and cook: a firm head with a pink blush, a few yellow tips or a small brown bruise. Trim the bruised or yellow parts. Yellowing heads may taste bitter, so the earlier you cook it, the better.
  • Trim hard: a head with brown, dried out edges but a firm, white center.
  • Throw it out: slimy or wet patches, a sour or off smell, fuzzy mold, or a head that has gone soft and brown all through. NCAT links slimy spots to bacterial blotch, and the 2025 storage study saw visible spoilage by day 7 at room temperature (Silva et al. 2025). If you are not sure, do not eat it.

How to keep your next lion's mane flush white

  1. Set light to about 200 lux for 12 hours a day, or less. Room light or a bright window with no direct sun is enough. Our lion's mane profile runs 190 lux on a 12 hour cycle.
  2. Keep the room in the 16 to 20 °C (60 to 68 °F) range NCAT gives for fruiting. Our profile fruits at 17 °C (63 °F).
  3. Keep humidity at about 90% while fruiting and 94% while pinning, the settings in our profile, inside the 85 to 95% NCAT recommends.
  4. Give it gentle fresh air, not a draft. Our profile runs 25 seconds of fan every 18 minutes. Move the kit away from vents and fans. The fresh air calculator sizes it for a closed chamber.
  5. Harvest when the spines have grown out but before the tips yellow. Lift and cut by the base so you never squeeze the spines.
  6. Cool it right away. Store it at 34 to 38 °F (1 to 3 °C) in a paper bag, and cook it within a few days.

If the pink comes back under 200 lux and 12 hours, the strain is probably one that blushes. Our dense white heads profile runs about 46 lux, which is closer to the 35 lux run that came out fully white in the 2025 study.

Why does light change lion's mane color at all?

Lion's mane uses light as a signal to form and shape the head, not for energy. That is why it needs some light but not much. In the 2025 study, the brighter treatment also pulled more selenium into the outer layer of the head, the side facing the light (Jozifek et al. 2025). The authors suggest light hitting the surface directly may drive that. They call their light results a pilot and say more work on light intensity and color is needed, so treat 200 lux and 12 hours as a tested starting point, not a law. Do mushrooms need light? has the light numbers for 20 species, and humidity and fresh air explains how damp air and fresh air trade off.

FAQ

Why is my lion's mane pink?

Usually light stress, and only on some strains. A 2025 study got pink young heads at 500 lux for 24 hours a day and white heads at 200 lux or less on a 12 hour cycle. The pink faded slightly as the heads matured.

Is pink lion's mane bad?

The study treats it as a stress color, not spoilage. A firm, fresh smelling pink head is a looks issue. Slime, a sour smell or mold are the signs to throw it out, whatever the color.

Why is my lion's mane turning yellow?

Age if it is the spine tips on a mature head, dry or drafty air if it is one side, and too much water if the yellow patches are wet or slimy. Harvest yellowing heads now, since yellowing lion's mane can taste bitter.

Why did my lion's mane turn brown in the fridge?

Enzymatic browning from age or bruising. It goes much faster when warm: in a 2025 study, lion's mane at 21 °C changed color past the considerable line by day 4, while at 5 °C it stayed close to white for a week.

How do I stop lion's mane from bruising?

Handle it by the base, never squeeze the spines, do not stack heads, and cool it quickly in a paper bag rather than sealed plastic.

How long does fresh lion's mane last?

About a week in the fridge. A 2025 study kept microbe counts acceptable until day 7 at 5 °C, and NCAT says most fresh mushrooms last 5 to 7 days, lion's mane sometimes a little longer.

item.title: Are mushroom spores legal in the United States?
item.description: Federal law does not list spores, but California, Florida, Georgia and Idaho do. State by state status for spores and psilocybin, each row cited and dated.
item.content:encoded:
Federally, mostly yes. Psilocybin and psilocin are Schedule I under 21 CFR 1308.11, but spores are not listed because they contain neither compound, and DEA has said so in writing. States differ. Idaho lists spores and mycelium as Schedule I. Georgia lists them as a dangerous drug. California and Florida make it a crime to sell, give away or transport them (California also bars cultivating them to produce psilocybin). Everywhere else I found no spore specific statute as of 2026-11-09, but that silence is not permission, because growing the mushroom is still a drug offense in 47 states plus DC.

Short answer

Spores are not a controlled substance under federal law. Psilocybin and psilocin are. The gap between those two facts is where the state laws live.

This post is a research summary, not legal advice. I checked every row below against a statute, a legislature page, an agency page or a dated legal review on 2026-11-09. Shroom Labs does not sell spores, cultures or psilocybin products, and nothing here is a cultivation guide. If you plan to act on any of it, read the statute for your state and talk to a lawyer.

What does federal law say about spores?

Federal law lists the chemicals, not the fungus. 21 CFR 1308.11(d) puts psilocybin (code 7437) and psilocyn (code 7438) in Schedule I. The text does not name spores, mycelium or mushrooms.

DEA addressed spores directly in a 2014 letter from its Drug and Chemical Evaluation Section. The position, as summarized by the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association (LAPPA), is that spores are not Schedule I because they do not contain psilocybin or psilocin. The same summary notes the other half of the position: once spores germinate and grow into mushrooms that contain psilocybin, that material is a controlled substance under the Controlled Substances Act.

So the federal line sits at the mushroom, not at the spore. That is also why intent matters so much in practice. A spore print on a microscope slide and a spore syringe sold for growing are the same biology, but a state legislature can treat them very differently.

Which states make spores illegal?

Four states address psilocybin spores or mycelium directly. I read the text for each one.

  • Idaho. Idaho Code 37-2705(d)(34) lists "spores or mycelium capable of producing mushrooms that contain psilocybin or psilocin" in Schedule I, next to psilocybin and psilocyn themselves. The section was last amended in 2026 (chapter 90) and the spore line is still there. This is the strictest spore rule I found, because the spores are the scheduled substance.
  • Georgia. O.C.G.A. 16-13-71 defines "dangerous drug" to include mushroom spores that contain psilocybin or psilocin when mature. Section 16-13-72 makes it unlawful to sell, give away, barter, exchange, distribute or possess a dangerous drug outside the licensed channels. Spores are not a Schedule I controlled substance in Georgia, but there is no microscopy carve out in the text.
  • California. Health and Safety Code 11390 makes it a crime to cultivate spores or mycelium with intent to produce psilocybin or psilocin. Section 11391 covers transporting, importing, selling, furnishing or giving them away to facilitate that cultivation. Both carry up to a year in county jail or state prison. The code also allows approved research, instruction or analysis through the state Research Advisory Panel.
  • Florida. Fla. Stat. 500.75, in effect since July 1, 2025, makes it a first degree misdemeanor to transport, import, sell, furnish or give away spores or mycelium capable of producing mushrooms that will contain psilocybin or psilocyn. Unlike California, the text does not mention intent. Possession is not on the list of prohibited acts.

How the four states compare, verb by verb

GeorgiaProhibited (dangerous drug)ProhibitedProhibited as distributionNot named, but the mushroom is Schedule I
CaliforniaNot namedProhibited if it facilitates cultivationProhibited if it facilitates cultivationProhibited with intent to produce psilocybin
FloridaNot namedProhibitedProhibitedNot named, but the mushroom is Schedule I

This table is my own reading of the statutes, so check the actual text before relying on it.

Is psilocybin itself legal anywhere in the US?

Not in the sense most people mean. No state has legalized general private use. What exists is a mix of decriminalization, deprioritization and tightly regulated programs, and psilocybin remains Schedule I federally in all of them.

LAPPA's November 2025 summary counts Schedule I status in 47 states, the District of Columbia and the five territories. Alaska puts all psychedelics in Schedule II and Maine uses its own Schedule X. Oregon and New Mexico exempt psilocybin handled under their regulated programs.

Legal status by jurisdiction, dated and cited

Every row below was checked on 2026-11-09. "Source date" is the date of the page or edition I relied on, which can be older than my check.

AlaskaSchedule II for all psychedelicsNo spore specific statute foundLAPPA, Nov 2025
CaliforniaSchedule I, misdemeanor possession. Six cities deprioritize enforcement, which is no defense in a state caseCultivation with intent and facilitating sales are crimes (HSC 11390, 11391)HSC 11390, HSC 11391, The Psilocybin Record, reviewed 2026-10-20
ColoradoAdults 21 and older may use, possess and cultivate for personal use. Licensed healing centers also operate. HB26-1325 (effective 2026-08-12) bars sales for pay and advertisingNo spore specific statute foundHB26-1325, signed 2026-06-04 and bill text
District of ColumbiaNot legal. Police must treat adult, non commercial activity as a lowest enforcement priority (Initiative 81)No spore specific statute foundD.C. Code 48-921.52
FloridaSchedule ITransport, import, sell, furnish or give away is a first degree misdemeanorFla. Stat. 500.75 (2026)
GeorgiaSchedule I (O.C.G.A. 16-13-25). Two 2026 laws did not legalize itMature psilocybin spores are a dangerous drug (O.C.G.A. 16-13-71, 16-13-72)Justia, O.C.G.A. 16-13-71 and The Psilocybin Record, reviewed 2026-08-01

New JerseyOne ounce or less is a disorderly persons offense, which is still a criminal offenseNo spore specific statute foundP.L. 2021, c.9
New MexicoSchedule I, with an exemption for the state Medical Psilocybin Act. The health department targets full implementation by 2027-12-31No spore specific statute foundNM Department of Health
OregonSchedule I, with an exemption for licensed psilocybin services under ORS 475A. Clients must be 21 or older and use at a licensed service centerNo spore specific statute foundOregon Health Authority
Connecticut, Utah, WashingtonSchedule I outside narrow medical or pilot programsNo spore specific statute foundLAPPA, Nov 2025

Two limits on this table. First, "no spore specific statute found" means I did not find one in the sources above, not that none exists. Second, states without a spore statute still criminalize the mushroom.

What changed in 2026?

A few things worth knowing, all from the sources in the table.

  • Colorado narrowed its personal use protection. HB26-1325 says personal use does not cover selling natural medicine for pay, advertising it, or using paid harm reduction services to run sales. Sharing with adults 21 and older in the listed contexts stays protected.
  • Georgia passed two psychedelic bills that do not legalize anything. One excepts an FDA approved form of psilocybin from Schedule I only if federal approval and rescheduling happen. The other sets clinic rules. Psilocybin stays Schedule I.
  • California still prohibits psilocybin. Two 2026 bills that name it were held in committee, and city level deprioritization does not change state law.
  • Idaho kept its spore line through a 2026 amendment of the Schedule I section.

Why is the spore question confusing?

Most "spores are legal" pages repeat the federal point and stop. Three things get lost.

  1. Federal silence is not state permission. Four states wrote spore rules and they are not alike. Idaho treats spores as the drug. Florida and California regulate what you do with them.
  2. The offense is usually the mushroom, not the spore. Where spores are lawful to hold, a grown cubensis or cyanescens flush is still a Schedule I material. The spore is legal only until it is used.
  3. Sellers do not decide your exposure. A vendor's "for microscopy only" label does not change what your state's statute says, so I would not assume it protects a buyer.

For the species we profile, the legal notice is the same on each page: Golden Teacher and P. cyanescens are listed as research references, not growing instructions. If your interest is culinary, none of this applies. Spores and cultures for oysters, lion's mane and shiitake are not controlled anywhere in the table. Start with growing mushrooms at home or cloning store-bought oysters.

FAQ

Are psilocybin mushroom spores legal federally?

Yes in the narrow sense that they are not listed in the federal schedules. 21 CFR 1308.11 names psilocybin and psilocyn, not spores, and a 2014 DEA letter says spores are not Schedule I because they contain neither compound. Growing them into mushrooms that contain psilocybin creates a controlled substance.

Which states ban psilocybin spores?

Four: California, Florida, Georgia and Idaho. Idaho lists spores and mycelium as Schedule I. Georgia classes them as a dangerous drug. California and Florida criminalize selling, giving away or transporting them, and California also criminalizes cultivating them to produce psilocybin.

Is it legal to own spores for microscopy?

Federally nothing in the schedules covers spores. In Idaho and Georgia the statutes have no microscopy exception that I could find. In California and Florida the text targets cultivation and sales or transport, not possession alone, and California separately allows approved research. State law and enforcement vary, so check your state's statute.

Is psilocybin legal in Colorado and Oregon?

Both run regulated programs, but they work differently. Colorado allows adults 21 and older personal use, possession and cultivation, plus licensed healing centers, and its 2026 update bars sales for pay and advertising. Oregon allows psilocybin only through licensed service centers under ORS 475A. Both remain subject to federal Schedule I status.

Are culinary mushroom spores legal everywhere?

Spores of culinary species such as oyster, lion's mane and shiitake do not contain psilocybin, and none of the spore statutes above reach them. Georgia's rule, for example, applies to spores of mushrooms that contain psilocybin or psilocin when mature.

Does a city decriminalization resolution protect me?

No. In California, six cities told police to treat psilocybin as a low priority, but the state's own law still applies and a city resolution is not a defense in a state prosecution.
